newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's Quinn hopeful on stability pact details.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Quinn hopeful on stability pact details.

text.p: Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn voiced guarded optimism on Wednesday that next week's European Union finance ministers' gathering would agree final details on a stability pact to underpin EMU.
Quinn told the Irish senate "it will not be an easy matter to resolve but I am cautiously optimistic that it will be possible to settle it".

The Irish minister, whose country holds the revolving EU presidency until the year's end, said that if the ministers failed to agree at their meeting on December 12, a summit meeting on December 13 and 14 in Dublin might reach an accord.
Next Thursday's meeting was called to clear up details of the pact to underpin economic and monetary union which were not decided at a similar ECOFIN meeting in Brussels this week.
The stability pact is a mechanism whhich would prevent countries which join EMU running up excessive budget deficits. Countries which did not meet agreed standards would be warned, then fined.
Quinn said the major outstanding issue was how to define when a government was running up an "exceptional" government deficit.

EU ministers have yet to agree how to define the "exceptional or temporary" circumstances which would allow a country to run up a budget deficit above an agreed upper limit of three percent of its gross domestic product.

Germany, architect of the stability pact, and the Netherlands, insist that there must be a strict, numerical definitition of such circumstances for fear that any other option could lead to political fudging which would weaken EMU.
Under the stability pact, fines will be imposed against member states if they overshoot agreed limits.
Quinn said the sanctions would be enforced in the form of non-interest bearing deposits which would be converted into a fine after two years if the excessive deficit persisted.
He told the Senate that the amount of the deposit would be made of a fixed component equal to one tenth of the excess of the deficit over the three percent reference value.
There would be an upper limit of 0.5 percent of GDP for the annual ammount of deposits, he said.

Quinn said sanctions were aimed more at deterring excess deficits than punishing them, "thus providing a very strong foundation for the euro and creating the conditions in which low interest rates can be consistent with price stability."
The single euro currency is to be adopted by member states which qualify for EMU and is to come into use by 2002 at the latest.
A draft sample of euro notes is to be unveiled by the Irish Central Bank during the EU summit -- and the idea of a euro currency for Ireland is to be tried out on the Irish public next week.

Quinn said to help familiarise people with the currency, supermarkets and pubs will display their prices both in Irish punts and the euro. A nominal rate of one euro to 80 Irish pence will be used as "an easy figure to work with," he said.
